```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Run the chunks in order. The input is a filtered 10x Genomics count matrix on the
course system. Update the path below if your data are elsewhere. Rows represent
genes and columns represent cells.

Load the packages used in this analysis:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(DropletUtils)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(DelayedMatrixStats)
library(uwot) # UMAP dimensionality reduction
library(Rtsne)
library(scran)
library(scater)
library(iSEE)
```

# Import the data

- Import the count matrix with `DropletUtils::read10xCounts()`.
  Use a named vector for `samples` to give each sample a short label.
  What changes if you leave the vector unnamed?

```{r}
library(DropletUtils)
sce <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(samples = c(
    "filtered" = "/project/shared/r/2_r_single_cell/4-bioconductor/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/"
))
```

> Answer:
>
> Without a vector name, the input path is used in the `Sample` column of the cell metadata.

- Print the object.
  What can you tell about its contents?

```{r}
sce
```

> Answer:
>
> The summary shows the object class, dimensions (genes by cells), and assay names.
> It also lists gene and cell names, metadata fields, reduced dimensions,
> and any alternative experiments.

- What can you tell from the object metadata?

**Note:** Use `metadata()` for experiment metadata, `rowData()` for gene metadata,
and `colData()` for cell metadata.

```{r}
metadata(sce)
```

> Answer:
>
> The `Samples` metadata field records the input path for each sample.

# Quality control

- Compute quality control (QC) metrics with `scuttle`: library size (total UMI
  count), number of genes detected, and mitochondrial percentage.

**Hint:** Identify mitochondrial genes and pass the logical vector to `subsets`.
The `MT-` prefix matches human gene symbols; other annotations may differ.

```{r}
is.mito <- grepl("^MT-", rowData(sce)$Symbol)
table(is.mito)
```

```{r}
library(scuttle)
sce <- scuttle::addPerCellQC(sce, percent.top = 50, subsets = list(MT = is.mito))
colnames(colData(sce))
```

- What is the return value?
  Where are the quality metrics stored?
  How does this differ from `scuttle::perCellQCMetrics()`?

> Answer:
>
> `addPerCellQC()` returns the object with QC metrics added to `colData(sce)`.
> `perCellQCMetrics()` returns a table without updating the object.
>
> - `sum`: total UMI count in the main experiment.
> - `detected`: number of genes with non-zero counts.
> - `percent.top_50`: percentage of counts assigned to the 50 most abundant genes.
> - `subsets_MT_sum`: total mitochondrial UMI count.
> - `subsets_MT_percent`: percentage of counts assigned to mitochondrial genes.
> - `total`: total UMI count across the main and any alternative experiments.
>
> High mitochondrial percentages or counts concentrated in a few genes can indicate
> poor cell quality. Interpret these metrics together.

- Visualise library size, genes detected, and mitochondrial percentage as three violin plots; use `ggplot2`.

```{r}
plot1 <- colData(sce) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_violin(aes(Sample, sum)) +
    labs(x = "Sample", y = "Total UMI count")
plot2 <- colData(sce) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_violin(aes(Sample, detected)) +
    labs(x = "Sample", y = "Genes detected")
plot3 <- colData(sce) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_violin(aes(Sample, subsets_MT_percent)) +
    labs(x = "Sample", y = "Mitochondrial counts (%)")
cowplot::plot_grid(plot1, plot2, plot3, nrow = 1)
```

- Filter cells, keeping those with more than 4,500 UMIs, less than 15% mitochondrial counts, and more than 1,500 genes detected.
  These thresholds are specific to this example; inspect QC distributions before
  choosing thresholds for another dataset.

```{r}
sce <- sce[, sce$sum > 4500 & sce$subsets_MT_percent < 15 & sce$detected > 1500]
sce
```

- Similarly, use `scuttle::perFeatureQCMetrics()` or `scuttle::addPerFeatureQC()` to compute per-feature quality metrics, and visualise those metrics.

**Hint:** Plot the number of cells with non-zero counts against the log10 mean count.
Genes with zero counts in all retained cells have an undefined log10 mean and are
omitted from this plot.

```{r}
sce <- scuttle::addPerFeatureQC(sce)
```

> Answer:
>
> The return value of `scuttle::addPerFeatureQC()` is a `SingleCellExperiment` object.
> The quality metrics are stored in the `rowData` component of the object.
> - `mean`: mean count per gene across retained cells.
> - `detected`: percentage of retained cells with non-zero counts per gene.

```{r}
rowData(sce) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    filter(mean > 0) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(detected / 100 * ncol(sce), log10(mean))) +
    labs(x = "Cells with non-zero counts", y = "Log10 mean count")
```

# Normalisation

- Use `scuttle::logNormCounts()` to adjust for library size and log-transform
  normalised counts. This reduces cell-specific differences in sequencing depth
  or capture efficiency.

```{r}
sce <- scuttle::logNormCounts(sce)
assayNames(sce)
```

- What is the return value?
- Where can you find the normalised counts?

> Answer:
>
> The return value of `scuttle::logNormCounts()` is a `SingleCellExperiment` object.
> Log-normalised counts are stored in the `"logcounts"` assay.
> The original counts remain in the `"counts"` assay.

## Bonus

- Plot variance against mean expression for raw and log-normalised counts.

```{r}
library(DelayedMatrixStats)
# Summarise raw counts.
x <- DelayedArray(assay(sce, "counts"))
plot_data <- tibble(
    mean = DelayedMatrixStats::rowMeans2(x),
    variance = DelayedMatrixStats::rowVars(x)
)
plot_counts <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(mean, variance)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Raw counts", x = "Mean count", y = "Variance")
# Summarise log-normalised counts.
x <- DelayedArray(assay(sce, "logcounts"))
plot_data <- tibble(
    mean = DelayedMatrixStats::rowMeans2(x),
    variance = DelayedMatrixStats::rowVars(x)
)
plot_logcounts <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(mean, variance)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Log-normalised counts", x = "Mean log-expression", y = "Variance")
cowplot::plot_grid(plot_counts, plot_logcounts, nrow = 1)
```

- How does the mean-variance relationship change?
  See [OSCA: quantifying per-gene variation](https://www.bioconductor.org/books/3.19/OSCA.basic/feature-selection.html#quantifying-per-gene-variation).

> Answer:
>
> Log-transformation reduces the influence of large counts, but a mean-variance
> relationship usually remains. These plots alone do not establish whether
> normalisation was effective; we model this relationship during feature selection.

# Feature selection

Select highly variable genes (HVGs) with `scran` for downstream analysis.

- Use `scran::modelGeneVar()` to model the variance of the log-expression profiles for each gene.
  Make sure to assign the output of the function to a new object (i.e. NOT `sce`).
  What is the output?

```{r}
library(scran)
dec <- scran::modelGeneVar(sce)
dec
```

> Answer:
>
> A `DataFrame` with one row per gene: mean log-expression, total variance,
> estimated technical and biological variance, p-values, and false discovery rates (FDRs).
>
> The p-values test whether biological variance is greater than zero; FDRs adjust
> for testing many genes.

- Use `scran::getTopHVGs()` to identify highly variable genes (e.g., top 10%).

What is the output?
How many genes do you identify?
Where are those genes in the plot of mean expression against biological variance?
What happens to this plot if you set more stringent thresholds to define highly variable genes?

```{r}
# Select up to 10% of all genes, requiring positive biological variance.
hvg <- scran::getTopHVGs(dec, prop = 0.1)
length(hvg)
```

```{r}
dec %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(
        gene_id = rownames(dec),
        hvg = gene_id %in% hvg
    ) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(mean, bio, color = hvg))
```

> Answer:
>
> Output of `scran::getTopHVGs()` is a character vector of feature identifiers.
>
> `length(hvg)` gives the number selected. These genes have the highest estimated
> biological variance and appear towards the top of the plot. Reducing `prop`
> selects fewer genes; the variance estimates and point positions stay the same.

## Bonus

- Plot mean expression against total (black), biological (blue), and technical
  (red) variance.

How do you interpret those different values?

```{r}
ggplot(as_tibble(dec)) +
    geom_point(aes(mean, total), color = "black") +
    geom_point(aes(mean, bio), color = "blue") +
    geom_point(aes(mean, tech), color = "red")
```

> Answer:
>
> - Total variance: observed variance in log-expression across cells.
> - Technical variance: variance estimated from the fitted mean-variance trend.
> - Biological variance: total variance minus estimated technical variance.
>
> Negative biological estimates occur when observed variance falls below the trend;
> they do not represent negative physical variation.

# Dimensionality reduction

- Apply principal component analysis (PCA) with `scran::fixedPCA()`.
  List the names of dimensionality reduction results available.

**Note:** Use only the HVGs to focus PCA on informative genes and reduce computation.
Set a seed for reproducible results when using randomised methods.

```{r}
set.seed(1234) # For randomised PCA methods
sce <- scran::fixedPCA(sce, subset.row = hvg)
reducedDimNames(sce)
```

- Compute UMAP and t-SNE from the PCA coordinates. Both produce two-dimensional
  layouts that help visualise similarities between cells.
  List the names of dimensionality reduction results available each time.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
sce <- runUMAP(sce, dimred = "PCA", external_neighbors = TRUE)
reducedDimNames(sce)
```

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
sce <- runTSNE(sce, dimred = "PCA", external_neighbors = TRUE)
reducedDimNames(sce)
```

**Note:** `external_neighbors = TRUE` uses an external nearest-neighbour search.
See `?scater::runUMAP` and `?scater::runTSNE` for details.

- Visualise the cell coordinates and colour points by a QC metric.
  The example below uses UMAP; try PCA and t-SNE as well.

```{r}
sce_umap <- reducedDim(x = sce, type = "UMAP") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    bind_cols(colData(sce) %>% as_tibble()) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = subsets_MT_percent)) +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
sce_umap
```

## Bonus

- Use `scran::denoisePCA()` to remove principal components that correspond to technical noise, and compare downstream t-SNE or UMAP with those obtained before denoising.

**Note:** Denoising retains enough PCs to capture the estimated biological
variation, subject to limits such as `min.rank`.

- Name the output `sce_denoise`.
- How many components remain after denoising?
- Visualise a UMAP of the denoised PCA and compare.

```{r}
sce_denoise <- scran::denoisePCA(sce, dec, subset.row = hvg)
ncol(reducedDim(sce_denoise, "PCA"))
```

> Answer:
>
> Read the number of retained PCs from the output above. In the original example,
> five were retained, which is also the default minimum (`min.rank = 5`).

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
sce_denoise <- scater::runUMAP(sce_denoise, dimred = "PCA", external_neighbors = TRUE)
reducedDimNames(sce_denoise)
```

```{r}
sce_denoise_umap <- reducedDim(x = sce_denoise, type = "UMAP") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    bind_cols(colData(sce_denoise) %>% as_tibble()) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = subsets_MT_percent)) +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
plot_grid(
    sce_umap + theme(legend.position = "bottom"),
    sce_denoise_umap + theme(legend.position = "bottom"),
    nrow = 1)
```

> Answer:
>
> Compare local structure between the layouts. A group visible in only one layout
> needs further investigation before it can be interpreted biologically.

# Clustering

Cluster cells using `scran`.

- Use `scran::getClusteredPCs()` to compare clustering across different numbers of
  PCs and suggest a number to retain.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
output <- scran::getClusteredPCs(reducedDim(sce, "PCA"))
metadata(output)$chosen
```

**Note:** This heuristic uses the number of clusters found at each PCA dimension.
Treat the suggested number as a starting point and compare other choices.

- Build a shared nearest-neighbour (SNN) graph using the suggested number of PCs,
  then cluster it with the Louvain method. Store cluster labels in `colData(sce)$label`.

```{r, message=FALSE}
set.seed(1234)
g <- scran::buildSNNGraph(t(reducedDim(sce, "PCA")), d = metadata(output)$chosen)
colData(sce)[["label"]] <- factor(igraph::cluster_louvain(g)$membership)
```

- Visualise the assigned cluster on your preferred dimensionality reduction layout.

**Note:** Clustering and UMAP both use PCA coordinates but serve different purposes.
A visual gap does not prove that groups are distinct cell types. Compare markers
and check whether the result is sensitive to parameter choices.

```{r}
gg_snn <- reducedDim(x = sce, type = "UMAP") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    bind_cols(colData(sce) %>% as_tibble()) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = label)) +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
gg_snn
```

## Bonus

- Test different numbers of principal components and compare results.

```{r, message=FALSE}
set.seed(1234)
snn_plots <- list()
for (d in c(5, 10, 13, 15)) {
    g <- scran::buildSNNGraph(t(reducedDim(sce, "PCA")), d = d)
    colData(sce)[["snn_d"]] <- factor(igraph::cluster_louvain(g)$membership)
    gg_d <- reducedDim(x = sce, type = "UMAP") %>%
        as.data.frame() %>%
        as_tibble() %>%
        bind_cols(colData(sce) %>% as_tibble()) %>%
        slice_sample(prop = 1) %>%
        ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = snn_d), size = 0.2) +
        labs(title = paste(d, "PCs")) +
        cowplot::theme_cowplot()
    snn_plots[[as.character(d)]] <- gg_d
}
plot_grid(plotlist = snn_plots, ncol = 2)
```

- Try `scran::quickCluster()` and compare the groups with the Louvain clusters.
  Inspect `?scran::quickCluster`, especially `min.size` and `use.ranks`. This function
  creates groups for normalisation; they are not necessarily cell types.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
sce$quickCluster <- scran::quickCluster(sce)

gg_cluster <- reducedDim(x = sce, type = "UMAP") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    bind_cols(colData(sce) %>% as_tibble()) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = quickCluster)) +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
gg_cluster
```

# Cluster markers

- Use `scran::findMarkers()` to identify markers for each cluster.
  Display the metadata of markers for the first cluster.

```{r}
markers <- scran::findMarkers(x = sce, sce$label, direction = "up", pval.type = "all")
rowData(sce)[rownames(markers[[1]]), ] %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    head()
```

**Note:** With `direction = "up"`, markers have higher expression in the target
cluster. `pval.type` controls which comparisons support a marker:

- `"all"`: higher expression than every other cluster (used here).
- `"any"`: higher expression than at least one other cluster.
- `"some"`: higher expression than a specified proportion of other clusters,
  controlled by `min.prop` (default: half).

See the function's help page for details of `findMarkers()`.

The clusters were derived from the same data, so treat marker p-values as
exploratory evidence. Use expression patterns and prior knowledge to interpret clusters.

Visualise the expression of selected markers:

- As individual cell expression values overlaid on violin plots.
  The example gene ID below is specific to this dataset; alternatively, select
  a gene from `rownames(markers[[1]])`.

```{r}
# Alternative: marker_id <- rownames(markers[[1]])[1]
marker_id <- "ENSG00000271503"
marker_name <- rowData(sce)[marker_id, "Symbol"]
colData(sce) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(marker = assay(sce, "logcounts")[marker_id, ]) %>%
    ggplot(aes(label, marker)) +
    geom_violin(aes(fill = label)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = marker_id, subtitle = marker_name,
         x = "Cluster", y = "Log-normalised expression")
```

- On a dimensionality reduction layout.
  Compare with the cluster labels.

```{r}
gg_marker <- reducedDim(x = sce, type = "UMAP") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(marker = assay(sce, "logcounts")[marker_id, ]) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = marker), size = 0.1) +
    scale_color_viridis_c() +
    labs(title = marker_id, subtitle = marker_name) +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
plot_grid(gg_marker, gg_snn)
```

# Interactive visualisation

- Use `iSEE::iSEE()` to explore the object in an interactive web application.
  Run this chunk in an interactive R session to open the app; it will not launch
  while rendering the notebook.

```{r}
library(iSEE)
panelDefaults(Downsample = TRUE)
app <- iSEE(sce)
if (interactive()) {
    shiny::runApp(app)
}
```

## Bonus

- Choose the panels shown when the application starts. Panel widths add up to
  12 per row, so the third panel starts a new row.

```{r}
initial_panel_list <- list(
    ReducedDimensionPlot(PanelWidth = 4L),
    RowDataTable(PanelWidth = 8L),
    ReducedDimensionPlot(PanelWidth = 4L)
)
app <- iSEE::iSEE(sce, initial = initial_panel_list)
if (interactive()) {
    shiny::runApp(app)
}
```
